replying_to: Replying to For Manifold Learning, Deep Neural Networks Can be Locality Sensitive Hash Functions
display_title: Official Review of Paper707 by Reviewer MTcC

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors define the notion of Geometry Sensitive Hashing (GSH) for neural networks evaluated on mixtures of manifolds, which is satisfied if the outputs of the neural network on any pair of points on the same manifold are close, and any pair of points on different manifolds are far.

They prove that this property holds under some particular conditions on the data distribution and neural network architecture.
content.main_review:
**Caveats:**
- I am not familiar with the literature in this area, so cannot determine the novelty of the results or whether there are missing citations.
- I did not read the proofs in detail, so cannot vouch for the correctness of the mathematical results.



**Review:**

*Please take my review with a pinch of salt, as I am not familiar with this area of work and so am perhaps missing some important context. (That said, perhaps my comments are still valuable if you would like the paper to be more accessible to a wider audience.)*


This was an interesting paper to review, as I was unsure whether to give it a very low rating or a very high rating. In the end I decided to go with the low rating, on the basis that this will give the reviewers an incentive to clarify my questions and comments, after which I may increase my rating. 

In brief, I'm not sure whether the results are "obvious"\* and therefore uninteresting, or are very profound, providing a handle to theoretically study very difficult and important questions about fundamental properties of neural networks. [\*I appreciate that even "obvious" things can be hard to prove, and it's clear to me that even if the results seem intuitive, actually proving them is non-trivial.]

In my mind, the results essentially boil down to saying: 
- very crudely: "neural networks can do classification"
- more verbosely: "neural networks can provably draw classification boundaries around distinct parts of the input space, and can learn to ignore irrelevant patterns across different classes so that new unseen classes are also well-separated, subject to assumptions on the input distribution and network architecture."

I'm not quite sure why the authors do not provide a more layman-friendly explanation of their results. As an example, being a Locality Sensitive Hash (LSH) basically just means that you are a good classifier, in that the buckets are the discrete classifier outputs. But this isn't stated in the paper, which makes things harder to understand. 

A few other comments in no particular order:
- I think the paper would benefit from having a candidate explanation of the assumptions that are being made on the data generating process, how this may differ from real-world data distributions, and -- importantly -- why it is reasonable to expect that the results of the paper would stem from these assumptions. E.g., in the linear case, it is essentially assumed that each manifold exhibits exactly the same structure, so from my layman perspective it seems kind of clear that the network would learn to be invariant to this intra-class structure, and therefore you would get one-shot learning (because one example is enough to get the representative of the class in the embedding space). 
- Why is the title of the paper about LSH, when the results are all about GSH? 
- The paper studies a very particular choice of architecture. What would happen with different architectures? 
- I believe the results all assume access to the population distributions (i.e. unlimited data). How might things change in the finite sample case?
- Would these results be straightforward if you assumed arbitrary function approximator neural networks rather than the particular choice of architecture? If so, aren't these results more about the particular architecture being studied, rather than neural networks in generality? (Not that this would be a huge problem, since proving anything for any neural network is great. But this should be made clear so that readers do not misunderstand the extent of the results.)




**Other random comments:**

Abstract: 
- I was a little confused by the statement: "Each input of a class is produced using two latent vectors", should it not be "output" since these are the things being generated?
- Please define the acronym LSH before using it the first time.



Page 3: 
- Start of Section 2. I was a little confused a few times whether the manifolds are discrete objects indexed by discrete values of \gamma, or whether they are supposed to be sub-manifolds of a higher dimensional manifold, indexed by a continuous variable \gamma. My understanding is that it is the former, and so the fact that the individual realisations of \gamma take value in a continuous space doesn't really matter -- they may as well be discrete. Is that correct, or have I overlooked something? Could you perhaps rephrase things to clarify either way?  [Edit: On further thinking, I suppose that if one makes assumptions about f, then assuming some geometry on \gamma does bring something non-trivial. Perhaps you could clarify that? And my initial confusion about whether the manifolds are discrete or continuously varying still stands.] 


Page 5:
- dim(A) = mxT, dim(B ) = TxD. Could you say what T is here? In particular, is T < m or T>= m? In the former case, it acts as a bottleneck. But in the latter case it doesn't do anything, so WLOG you could just have a single matrix here, no need for two. I am a bit confused why this is introduced, could you clarify this in the text for other readers?
content.summary_of_the_review:
Interesting paper to review, but unsure whether it is proving kind-of-obvious results in an over-formalised setup, or a really great paper that provides a handle on studying hard and very important problems. 

[Edit: raised score to marginally below after author response]

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper707 by Reviewer MTcC

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their review and feedback on our work. 

- Foremost, the main result is not about the final output of a neural network but rather about the penultimate layer and the function induced by. Note, that having LSH at the final layer does not necessitate LSH holding at the penultimate layer. Yet, we both show that GSH has great practical merits (e.g,. transferability and interpretability) and that NNs properly trained can achieve this property. 

- "Candidate explanation of the assumptions": While our distributional assumptions do not capture all the complexity of real-world data, it is still highly non-trivial to give a full characterization of how Neural Networks behave in simplified settings such as ours, especially so when such frameworks can shed light on real phenomena. While our ultimate goal is to improve the training process, it is important to understand that theoretical progress has to be made in steps.
- Reason for LSH in title as opposed to GSH: GSH is a term we introduce in our Section 1. To keep things clear to an unfamiliar reader, we decided to use LSH in the title.
- “The paper studies a particular architecture” Indeed, the exact choice of architecture is not crucial to our result. Rather a few salient properties are important, such as representation ability (this is achieved via the wide first layer), optimization ability (this is achieved via recent progress on characterizing minima in DNNs) and transfer learning (this is achieved by having more than one hidden layer). Deep over-parameterized architectures are also known to satisfy these properties. We chose a 3-layer architecture for simplicity of presentation.
- The results specifically do not assume access to population data. We have finite sample results. Due to space constraints we had to move the generalization bound analyses to the appendix.
- "Each input of a class is produced using two latent vectors", We apologize for the confusion - we referred to the generated point as input as that is fed to the supervised learning algorithm as an input.
- Are the results specific to our choice of architecture? We agree that our results are not limited to the specific architecture chosen and hold for more general architectures. However, we study what happens as a result of optimization dynamics in a non-convex setting, an intractable objective for arbitrary function approximator neural networks. That is, even if a NN has the expressive power to represent arbitrary functions, it might not be able to learn arbitrary functions using gradient based methods. We show a setting where the network provably does learn it.
- Confusion about continuity of manifolds: Our manifolds are discrete objects which are sampled from an underlying continuous distribution, quite similar to how one samples from a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Moreover, similar to how two samples from a continuous distribution are unlikely to lie very close to each other, two manifolds in our model defined by two \gammas sampled from a continuous distribution are unlikely to lie very close to each other.
- “dim(A) = mxT, dim(B ) = TxD. Could you say what T is here? In particular, is T < m or T>= m? In the former case, it acts as a bottleneck. But in the latter case it doesn't do anything, so WLOG you could just have a single matrix here, no need for two. I am a bit confused why this is introduced, could you clarify this in the text for other readers?”
    We apologize for the lack of clarity here. We will fix it. We intend T >=m. Having two linear layers with no non-linearity in between them is NOT the same as a single linear layer. Firstly, having two linear layers allows us to study the representations being computed by the network at the intermediate layer theoretically. Secondly, even though two linear layers doesn’t add representation power, the  optimization dynamics change drastically by adding the additional layer, e.g., see [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Linear Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00468). In fact, in the experiments we have performed replacing the fully connected layers of a CNN by two linear layers leads to an increase in accuracy of over 1% on CIFAR10. Hence two linear layers cannot be treated to be the same as a single linear layer in the context of DNN optimization.

We hope that our clarifications helped the reviewer see the paper in a clearer way and would be happy to address follow up questions.

content.title: Thanks for the response
content.comment: Thank you for the response, this clarifies my questions. However I am still not convinced that the paper is ready for publication, so I will raise my score to marginally below.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors mainly investigated whether deep neural networks learn salient features which are informative for classification, while non-informative noises are eliminated. To verify this, they first generate synthetic data that drawn from delicately designed manifold distributions, then levearge DNNs to invert the manifold geometry. They elaborated theoretical analysis to show the DNNs work as a GSH-like functions to map inputs from the same class to the similar embeddings while any two inputs from different class to distinct embeddings. As one of the desirable consequences of sensitive hashing mapping, they proposed to apply it to one-shot learning.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

- The motivation is meaningful. It aims to help us get better understanding of how DNNs works, thereby aids moudlar design of DNN systems.
- They proposed a reasonable data generating process to help in verifying their hypothesis that the DNNs work as GSH function to cluster input data. Besides, they also provided solid theoretical proof to show that.
- On the synthetic data, they prove that GSH holds not only for known manifolds but also for unseen manifolds leading to effective one-shot learning. 
- They conducted experiments to valid their work.

Weakness&major concerns:

- Although the theoretical part is sound and solid, the experiments are mainly conducted on synthetic data results in the work less convincing.
- Which loss has been used for training Myrtle-CNN on MNIST and CIFAR-10? Cross entrop loss or the proposed in eq (1)?
- Could you please train a DNN model for synthetic data instead of the proposed MLP model and get some experiment results of it? I am quite interested in how it performs on a regular model (instead of delicately designed one) when your data already satisfied strong assumptions.
- Is it possible to use some simple public benchmarks for one-shot learning? for instance omniglot.
- Since for CIFAR-10 GSH doesn't hold, could you please give some application scenario? or could you please clarify the merit of this work?

I would appreciate if the author can address my concerns and help me to see the impact of this work to the deep learning community.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work is quite interesting. Although the theoretical part is sound, the experiments are less convincing. Before my concerns are addressed, I recommend to weakly reject.

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for appreciating our motivation and theoretical analysis and address their comments regarding the empirical part below with the hope of convincing that real applications have a similar albeit non-identical underlying mechanism at play. 


- “The experiment were conducted mainly on synthetic data”. The main advantage of using synthetic datasets over real-world experiments is that we have a handle over the data generating function. Therefore, we can completely isolate a semantically meaningful feature to generates classes. Having this function for real datasets would allow us to generate classes of fine granularity that share minimal semantic similarity (e.g., Dalmatic dogs vs Aircraft carriers) a condition for GSH to hold *class-wise*. However, our (and other work, e.g., Neural Collapse) experiments demonstrate that there is some clustering phenomenon even for real distributions suggesting that while class-wise (neural) collapse is not happening perhaps there is some collapse in all the representations that share specific semantic features, for example, perhaps, all dark airplanes with blue skies have approximately the same representation (This would be hard to demonstrate empirically as we do not have such fine labels).
-  Which loss has been used? The loss for real experiments was Cross-Entropy and the final accuracy on CIFAR was ~89%. Our goal was to use well performing models to mimic real models on real distributions. 
- Could you please train a DNN model? The model trained on the synthetic data was a fully connected DNN model (a stronger version than the model we used in our theory). Nevertheless, to address the concerns of the reviewer we trained a ResNet18 on our synthetic data reshaped as images.  Somewhat surprisingly, this model performs even better in terms of GSH achieving $\rho=40$ for the synthetic distribution. We thank the reviewer for this suggestion and would add this experiment to the final version.
- Lack of few-shot experiments on real data: The reason we have not ran few shot learning experiments such as omniglot is that those experiments have been done in prior work. Our premise is to try to understand why is few-shot/transfer learning even possible and what assumptions our data have to satisfy to enable this phenomenon.
- Please give some application scenario? The main merit of our work is to shed light on what happens in the representation layer of NNs when our data is generated with the manifold assumption. Practically speaking this suggests a mechanism that would explain why we are able to generalize to unseen classes and data distributions. For example, a practitioner seeking to have good out-of-distribution performance could try to explore ways of achieving a strong GSH (perhaps via a similar regularization to our suggestion).

We hope that our clarifications helped the reviewer see the paper in a clearer way and would be happy to address follow up questions.

display_title: An additional response to the reviewer comment

content.title: An additional response to the reviewer comment
content.comment:
We want to emphasize that we are NOT claiming that today's DNNs satisfy GSH. Rather, our main message is that (a) GSH property is useful for many properties such as transfer learning, robustness, interpretability and (b) in simplified settings, at least, DNNs can exhibit GSH provably. 
Our experiments are intended to show that this is not a behavior that is totally out of line with what happens today in practice. In this regard, we show that GSH does indeed hold to a good extent with its effect weakening as we move to more complex datasets. Moreover, the experimental line of work on Neural Collapse shows very strongly that GSH holds on \emph{train} data across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets for CNNs and ResNets (50+ layers) and more architectures. We believe this to also be supporting evidence that GSH as a behavior is feasible to achieve with potentially minor tweaks to today's architectures. And doing so, has numerous benefits as we get a more robust, interpretable and modular building block for constructing complex AI systems which pass around representations to each other.
We ask that the reviewer view our paper in this manner. We are not trying to claim that GSH is already well-satisfied in today's networks across all architectures and datasets.

We thank the reviewer again for their time!

display_title: Official Review of Paper707 by Reviewer Xmdv

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates and analyzes how representations learned from supervised learning models behave as locality sensitive hash functions — this is such that they filter out nuisance factors of variability to learn invariant representations for classes — often leading to their superior performance on supervised tasks. The paper starts by studying a generative model of classes that is primarily defined by two latent factors — $\gamma$ and $\theta$, which, broadly speaking, correspond to the “content” and “style” of any given sample ‘x’. In other words, the goal of the learner is to “invert” the generative process and estimate $\gamma$ accurately while learning invariance to $\theta$. The paper provides theoretical evidence that with a few assumptions, representations learned by simple NNs are purely a function of $\gamma$. Moreover, the paper provides some evidence to suggest that this is beneficial for one-shot learning of previously unseen classes using a nearest neighbor lookup. The main contribution of the paper is to define, analyze Geometry Sensitive Hashing (GSH) for NNs mainly for the test distribution, and extending this idea to previously unseen classes.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
* The paper rigorously studies an important problem that is fundamental to most of supervised learning. 
* The formulation of the problem in the paper is quite interesting and well motivated. I liked the general framework of analyzing samples from a particular class on different manifolds, with representation learning primarily being posed as one of inverting this generative process. On simple datasets, even simple models trained this way appear to reflect the GSH property to some degree. 
* On synthetic, MNIST and CIFAR the proposed method demonstrates the GSH property to varying degrees.  

Weaknesses and Comments:
As I mentioned earlier, i thought this was an interesting theoretical paper that is explained fairly well. However, I have some reservations about some of the assumptions, terminology and experiments which I will try to outline here. 
* I find the basic generative model assumption to be quite simple — how realistic is the idea that every class lies on an separate manifold specified by $\gamma$? In this formulation is the assumption that a data manifold (say \mathcal{X}) is entirely defined as a cross-product space of these different manifolds? i.e., $\mathcal{X} \approx \gamma_1 \times \gamma_2 \times .. \gamma_m$ ? this is making an explicit assumption that attributes are not shared across classes which is untrue (for e.g., semantic features of a dog vs cat). 
* I dont entirely follow the nuance between why GSH properties of a test distribution must be very different from the training distribution, assuming both are drawn from the same underlying data distribution? This could be further clarified so as to also better outline the contributions of this work from those of Papyan et al., 2020 & Han et al., 2021. 
* Next, The claim on unseen classes can be evaluated more thoroughly. The current setup basically argues that since networks exhibit the GSH property, a single example from an unseen class is sufficient to learn to classify that class going ahead. However, even in CIFAR10 the GSH property doesn’t seem to hold — how does the one shot learning function in this case? Presumably the performance degrades significantly. Its hard to assess the broader applicability from just synthetic datasets. For MNIST given $\rho$ is sufficiently high, how does this compare with other few shot/one-shot techniques? 
* Throughout the paper, the current work on self supervised learning is largely overlooked. However, it strikes me as being extremely relevant to the formulation of the paper. The fact that many recent techniques are able to learn representations that perform extremely well even on ImageNet with just a linear classifier can be seen as a version of $B\sigma(C)$ in the formulation outlined in sec 4.2. Granted they are optimizing for a different objective like contrasting and/or consistency. In this regard, its not entirely clear to me why a weighted mean squared error cost in (1) is optimized instead of more commonly used objectives for classification.

A note on terminology: I found the word “manifold” is loosely defined here and quite confusing. It might help to explicitly define the manifold so as to avoid this confusion. For e.g. it is later stated that by fixing the functions ‘f’ to be a set of analytic functions, the different classes are all manifolds of shared geometry.. It’s not clear what this exactly means — does this mean the same distance metric is applicable across all the class-manifolds?What is the consequence of this? Aren’t these basically sub-manifolds of the data manifold $\mathcal{X}$ from which they inherit the metric. Isn’t a “linear” manifold just a subspace of the Euclidean space?
content.summary_of_the_review: This is quite a dense, yet well written paper. The paper presents rigorous analysis of representations learned by NNs and interprets them as locality sensitive hash functions that are excellent at preserving intra class vs inter class distances accurately; followed up by extensive theoretical analysis and some empirical studies. It's not clear to me from the paper how one extends this analysis to more complex settings. I would have liked to see if GSH holds on more commonly used modern networks (resnets for e.g.) on some of the standard benchmarks to draw insights. The claims on unseen classes are a bit weak in my opinion. They could be evaluated more thoroughly other than simply on synthetic data. I appreciate the link between GSH properties and one-shot learning, but the empirical studies do not seem to back this up entirely. Finally, it seems like a lot of the recent work in self supervised learning is closely related to this work, considering it is also unsupervised and potential connections with those methods maybe useful for the general reader.

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback on our work and for appreciating our motivation and set up. We try to address specific comments raised by the reviewer below:

- How realistic our data assumption? In general, a better way to model a class would be as a union of manifolds where each manifold is a semantic concept (e.g., having a nose). However, this assumption is much harder to model so we elect to simplify the setting to some extent where we view each gamma as a collection of all shared features (so the first coordinate could signify having a nose). Furthermore, if we had a handle on gamma for real data (if we had access to latents generating real images) then trying to learn each such gamma would produce GSH representations. 
- Why GSH train $\ne$ test? The behavior on a finite set of samples does not always carry on the population. A simple example, is train a large MLP (multilayer-perceptron) on Cifar10. The training-accuracy (will be 100%) and the test-accuracy (will be about 40-50%) will have a large gap. 
- Evaluating more thoroughly on unseen classes? We have two ways of thinking about it:
    - We can see GSH as an ideal goal but we (as a community) have not reached this point yet, especially so on complex datasets. Nevertheless, we show that GSH is possible and is a good goal to strive towards. Consider classifiers which achieve perfect accuracy, some are robust and some are non-robust, similarly some are fair while some are highly biased. Likewise, some models satisfy GSH and some do not. We propose GSH as a goal to strive towards on top of good accuracy.
    - The fact that we don’t see *class-wise-GSH* does not mean we do not get GSH at all, perhaps all dalmatians are mapped to the same representation. This would translate to transfer/few-shot learning, as the representation is able to extract semantically meaningful features, thus just doing Nearest-Neighbor in the embedding space will be a good few-shot learner.
- Connection to SSL: We agree that there is a deep connection with SSL and cited relevant works but our focus was on supervised learning so we kept the discussion limited. We will try to make it more descriptive. Regarding the loss function, we used a common loss (even for classification) for tractability purposes but believe our analysis should carry for more general losses. In our experimental studies we used cross entropy. 

We hope that our clarifications helped the reviewer see the paper in a clearer way and would be happy to address follow up questions.

content.title: Response to author's comments
content.comment:
I have read the authors response and other reviews for the paper. I am still of the opinion that the paper is not ready for publication in its current form. I will respond to each of the authors comments in detail below: 

* _Data assumption_: I agree that the the “true” manifold requires identifying disentangled representations — which is challenging but there are several works that have studied this in the context of generative models and classifiers. Moreover, do we expect trends to change if we use the ’right’ manifold assumption vs the more coarse one that is currently done? (For e.g. in CIFAR10). 

* _Test/Train_: Perhaps I was not clear, my question was that is there is no distribution shift between train and test, why should we expect GSH properties to vary significantly? Even if there is no overlap between the two distributions. 

* _Few/one shot_: I appreciate the clarification that GSH is an important property for DNNs like robustness. I think it might be more convincing to compare one-shot learning performance with standard datasets (I think one of the reviewers pointed to Omniglot) or other benchmarks — even if showing that DNNs that satisfy the GSH property do better on those benchmarks than those that do not.
